gbs333-aaa301-d1e104.summary: Title line of the whole work, announcing it as an 'Epitome and Collectorium' on the four books of the Sentences.

gbs333-aaa301-d1e122.summary: Biel's opening statement of purpose: the aim of theological study is a 'savoring' knowledge of God (sapida cognitio), which is true wisdom and which increases charity, the bond that unites the soul to God. Because Scripture is vast and difficult for beginners, Peter Lombard, like a busy bee gathering from the hives of the Fathers, assembled the Sentences as an ordered digest of theological doctrine with patristic testimonies, and later masters have built their scholastic disputations upon this order. The paragraph thus justifies both the study of theology and the choice of the Sentences as its framework.
claims: The end of theological study is a savoring knowledge of God, which is true wisdom and increases charity.
Charity alone makes us pleasing to God, perfects us, and unites us to him.
Because Scripture is vast and difficult, beginners should not be thrown into it directly.
Lombard's Sentences collect and order theological dogmas with patristic testimonies so that the reader need not search through many books.
Subsequent masters rightly adhere to Lombard's order and dispute theological questions around it.
concepts: theology as affective knowledge of God

gbs333-aaa301-d1e239.summary: Explains Biel's methodological choice: because commentators proceed by different and sometimes contrary routes, a student must choose one teacher to follow principally lest he wander without footing. Biel therefore commits himself to one doctrine that is more familiar to him, while still adducing other opinions when useful, and protests that he despises no orthodox author but honors all of them. He presents himself not as a master but as a fellow traveler, adopting Augustine's posture from De Trinitate of inquiring together and accepting correction.
claims: A student profits more by principally following one doctrinal path than by wandering among contrary ones.
Biel will chiefly follow one teacher but cite others when needed.
Biel disparages no orthodox and catholic writer; he will defend his own positions rather than attack others.
Biel writes as a co-inquirer, not as a master, and is willing to be corrected.

gbs333-aaa301-d1e344.summary: Names the chosen authority: Biel's project is to abridge the teaching of William of Ockham, the 'venerable inceptor', on the four books of the Sentences, raising scholastic questions on the prologue and each distinction. Where Ockham writes at length (especially in Book I) Biel will condense him; where Ockham says little or nothing, Biel will gather the opinions of other doctors that do not depart from Ockham's principles—hence the title 'Collectorium' and 'Epitome'. He also reserves the right to say things consistent with Ockham's principles even where Ockham seems to hold the opposite, and submits all his work to the judgment of the Church.
claims: Biel's work is an abridgment of Ockham's Sentences teaching.
Where Ockham is silent, Biel will supply the views of other doctors consistent with Ockham's principles.
The work is therefore called both 'collectorium' and 'epitome'.
Biel may sometimes argue from Ockham's principles to conclusions Ockham himself seems not to hold.
Biel submits all his writing to the correction of the Church and of better-informed orthodox readers.
concepts: fidelity to principles vs. to conclusions

gbs333-aaa301-d1e425.summary: Transitions to the prologue proper, which Biel will abridge from Ockham's prologue, and lays out its tripartite plan: theology is examined in itself, in relation to its unity, and in relation to its object.
claims: The prologue treats theology in three respects: in itself, in relation to its unity, and in relation to its object.
concepts: theology as a habitus under investigation

gbs333-aaa301-d1e445.summary: Specifies the first part of the plan: inquiry into what kind of knowledge theology is—whether it is a science or some other kind of cognition.
claims: The first inquiry concerns whether theology is a science or another kind of knowledge.

gbs333-aaa301-d1e452.summary: Specifies the second part of the plan: since the unity of a science derives from the unity of its subject, the inquiry into theology's unity becomes an inquiry into the subject of theology.
claims: The unity of a science is derived from the unity of its subject.
The second inquiry therefore concerns the subject of theology.

gbs333-aaa301-d1e459.summary: Specifies the third part of the plan—whether theology is practical or speculative, since the object of any science is either praxis or speculation—and announces that Biel will not pursue all of Ockham's questions at length, omitting or abbreviating those that are purely logical and referring the reader to Ockham where he is clear, for the sake of brevity.
claims: The third inquiry concerns whether theology is practical or speculative.
Purely logical questions in Ockham's prologue will be treated briefly or omitted.
Where Ockham is clear, Biel will simply refer to him.

gbs333-aaa301.summary: The preamble to Biel's Collectorium sets out the purpose, method, and plan of the whole commentary. Theology aims at a savoring knowledge of God that is true wisdom and increases charity; because Scripture is vast, Lombard's Sentences provide an ordered digest that scholastic masters have rightly followed. Since commentators diverge, Biel chooses one principal guide—William of Ockham—whose Sentences teaching he will abridge, filling Ockham's gaps with other doctors' views consistent with his principles, while professing respect for all orthodox authors, adopting Augustine's posture of shared inquiry, and submitting everything to the Church's correction. He then outlines the prologue's three inquiries, into theology's character as knowledge (science or not), its unity (hence its subject), and its object (practical or speculative), and warns that purely logical questions will be abbreviated.
claims: The end of theological study is a savoring, charity-increasing knowledge of God.
Biel's Collectorium is an epitome of Ockham's Sentences teaching, supplemented by other doctors consistent with Ockham's principles.
The prologue treats theology as knowledge, its unity through its subject, and its practical or speculative character.
